analysis.investment_thesis: Capri Global is a fast-growing NBFC with a 37% revenue CAGR, but this growth is funded almost entirely by debt (D/E of 2.52, borrowings up from INR 4,832 Cr to INR 15,577 Cr in three years) while finance costs compound at 68% per annum — far outpacing income growth. ROE of 11.8% on this level of leverage is deeply inadequate and the balance sheet is building risk faster than earnings justify.
key_strengths: Revenue CAGR of 37.2% and net profit CAGR of 30.4% over nine years show genuine business momentum in MSME/home loan/gold loan niches that are structurally under-served in India
Promoter holding of 59.92% with strong DII ownership of 20.09% signals institutional confidence and management alignment
Forward P/E of 12.96x reflects growth expectations already moderating to a more realistic pace, and if asset quality holds, the earnings trajectory could be meaningful
key_risks: Finance costs at INR 1,274 Cr grew 68% CAGR over nine years — compounding at nearly double the pace of revenue — this is the hallmark of a business where borrowing costs are cannibalising operating economics
ROE of 11.8% on D/E of 2.52 is an unacceptable combination; a conservatively leveraged NBFC should generate 18-22% ROE to justify the balance-sheet risk I would be accepting

No positive operating cash flow in any of the last five years — the AUM growth model is entirely dependent on continued access to wholesale debt markets; any credit market disruption could be severely destabilising
red_flags: D/E of 2.52 with borrowings tripling in three years (INR 4,832 Cr to INR 15,577 Cr) — this is classic aggressive expansion funded by debt, one of my hardest disqualifiers

OCF negative in all 5 of last 5 years — while NBFC loan deployment naturally creates negative OCF, the worsening trend (from -319 Cr to -4,312 Cr) shows acceleration of risk without proportional earnings improvement

Net profit was flat at INR 205 Cr for two consecutive years (FY22 and FY23) despite massive balance sheet growth — capital deployed far exceeded return generated; the recent FY25 profit jump needs several quarters of validation
analysis.detailed_analysis: In principle, a focused MSME and home-loan NBFC serving India's under-banked middle class is a business I could find interesting — it is consumer-facing, addresses a real credit gap, and has durable demand. But Capri Global is growing its loan book too fast, borrowing too aggressively, and not yet generating the ROE a leveraged financial institution must deliver to compensate for credit risk. When I look at the P&L, I see a business where almost every rupee of incremental equity raised is being deployed to grow the loan book, with minimal surplus returning to shareholders. The best NBFCs I have admired — Bajaj Finance, Cholamandalam — earned 20%+ ROE consistently before scaling. CGCL is scaling before it has proven that unit economics at scale.
